```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

You have two sets of results from the same papers: one the AI produced, one a
person produced by hand. You want to know how well the AI did.

The two tables can't simply be laid side by side, because people and AI often
describe the same thing in different ways. So ecoeval works in two steps. First
it **pairs up the rows**, matching each AI row to the human row describing the
same thing. Then it **scores the result**.

This guide covers the whole process. [Aligning records](aligning-records.html)
explains how the pairing works, and [Metrics](metrics.html) explains how the
numbers are computed.

## The five inputs

Four data inputs, two for each side, plus the schema:

|          | Paper list       | Record list        |
| -------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
| **AI**   | papers processed | records extracted  |
| **Gold** | papers reviewed  | records recorded   |

`schema.json`, the schema the AI extracted against, is **required**. It sets
how each column is compared by default, which values each column allows, and
which columns identify a record.

The paper lists are optional. They add papers to the comparison without
changing how anything is scored. Each list brings in papers that would
otherwise be left out:

| List supplied | Papers it adds                     | What that lets you catch |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Gold          | Human reviewed, found nothing      | AI **over**-extraction   |
| AI            | AI processed, found nothing        | AI **under**-extraction  |

For an ecoextract database you don't need to supply the AI paper list. ecoeval
reads it from the `documents` table, which lists every paper processed, whether
or not extraction produced records.

## Running it

```r
library(ecoeval)

# Launch and pick inputs in the app.
run_eval_app()

# Or supply them up front.
run_eval_app(
  ai          = "ecoextract_records.db",
  gold        = "gold_standard.csv",
  schema      = "ecoextract/schema.json",
  gold_papers = "papers_reviewed.csv"
)
```

The app walks through six stages, listed down the left side. You can go back to
any stage without redoing the ones after it:

1. **Load**: the five inputs
2. **Identify the papers**: which column identifies a paper, detected in this
   order: DOI, file name, title, first author and year
3. **Align papers**: which papers are compared
4. **Map record fields**: column mapping, comparisons, identity columns
5. **Compare**: one paper at a time, with the pairings and the results on one
   screen
6. **Dashboard**: overall metrics, updated as you review

### Skipping the setup screens

Every input a setup screen asks for can be passed to `run_eval_app()` instead.
The app runs the stages it has inputs for and opens on the first one it
doesn't. If you rerun the same evaluation after every prompt change, it can
open straight on the comparison:

```r
run_eval_app(
  ai             = records,               # a path, or a data frame shaped in R
  gold           = "gold_standard.csv",
  schema         = "ecoextract/schema.json",
  paper_key      = "doi",
  mapping        = list(gold = c(sample_size = "n_individuals")),
  linkage_fields = c("bat_species_scientific_name", "interaction_type"),
  comparator_config = data.frame(field = "location_country", comparator = "fuzzy"),
  normalizers    = list(location_country = function(x) countrycode_to_name(x)),
  judge          = NULL                   # no LLM calls this run
)
```

If you leave an input out, the app stops on its screen, filled in with
everything before it. With `skip_setup = TRUE` it takes the screen's defaults
instead (the detected paper key, the matcher's high-confidence paper links, the
suggested mapping, the schema's comparisons) and opens on the comparison.
`paper_map` supplies the paper links directly. With `auto_accept = FALSE` the
app stops on the paper-link review instead of accepting the confident links.

A normaliser converts both sides to a common form before matching and
comparison, for example turning a gold standard's codes into the wording the
documents use. The grid and its tooltips still show what each side actually
said, with the compared form beside it when the two differ. `skip` turns off
steps a run doesn't need: `"normalize"`, `"conformance"` (the schema check),
and `"granularity"`.

`evaluate_extraction()` takes the same arguments, so a scripted run and the app
can share one configuration.

To try it without any data of your own, press **Use the bundled example** on
the load screen. It reads the synthetic example data shipped with the package,
where each row tests a specific case.

## Without the app

Everything the app computes is also available as plain functions over data
frames, so you can run an evaluation from a script:

```{r}
library(ecoeval)

ex <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "ecoeval")

run <- evaluate_extraction(
  ai          = ex("ai_records.csv"),
  gold        = ex("gold_records.csv"),
  schema      = ex("schema.json"),
  ai_papers   = ex("ai_papers.csv"),
  gold_papers = ex("gold_papers.csv")
)
```

First, which papers were compared. Papers only one side covers are left out
and don't count against either side:

```{r}
str(run$scope)
```

Then the numbers:

```{r}
aggregate_metrics(run$cells)
record_metrics(run$pairs)
```

And the numbers for each column, worst first:

```{r}
field_metrics(run$cells)[, c("field", "n_scored", "accuracy", "precision", "recall")]
```

## Two ways to use it

**"How accurate is it?"** Press **Resolve all differences** on the dashboard.
The AI reviewer runs across every paper, the numbers fill in, and you don't
need to open a paper. This is the usual case.

**"Why is it wrong?"** Go through the papers, read the mismatches, and look for
patterns to fix before the next extraction run. Do this when you're changing
the schema or the prompt.

If you skip the review, you're accepting the matcher's pairings. A wrong
pairing barely moves the field-level metrics, but it does move record-level
precision and recall.

The dashboard shows how the numbers were produced:

```{r}
progress_summary(run$cells, run$scope$papers)
```

`n_pending_cells` counts cells the plain comparisons couldn't settle and the AI
reviewer hasn't read yet. For now they count as differences.

## Findings

Findings are grouped by where the fix belongs: the schema, the model, or the
gold standard. None of them change the metrics.

```{r}
run$findings[, c("group", "finding")]
```

The app only stops in two cases, because in either one there's nothing to
compare: the two sources share no papers, or no fields can be mapped between
the two record sets.

## Export

The export bundle and a saved session are the same files.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
export_bundle(
  "ecoeval_run_2026-08-31",
  cells  = run$cells,
  pairs  = run$pairs,
  config = capture_run_config(new_run_config(), comparators = run$config),
  scope  = run$scope,
  schema = run$schema
)
```

```
ecoeval_run_2026-08-31/
  aligned_table.csv        one row per aligned record, the values in full
  aligned_table_long.csv   tidy: one row per record x field, for pivoting
  metrics.xlsx             one sheet per field + summary sheet
  findings.csv             findings, grouped schema / model / gold
  schema_patch.json        proposed schema edits
  plots/                   column accuracy, per-field confusion matrices (PNG)
  run_config.json          mappings, comparators, linkage fields, judge verdict
                           cache, every manual link/reject decision, scope
  README.txt               what's here, which papers were compared, any warnings
```

`run_config.json` lets you reproduce a run. Pass it to
`run_eval_app(run_config = "...")` to pick up where you left off, with your
manual links and the AI reviewer's verdicts.

## Iterating

Two features help you improve the extraction from one run to the next.

**Compare a run with an earlier one.**

```{r}
before <- capture_run_config(new_run_config(),
                             metrics = list(record_f1 = 0.71, interaction_type = 0.62))
after  <- capture_run_config(new_run_config(),
                             metrics = list(record_f1 = 0.78, interaction_type = 0.91))
diff_runs(before, after)
```

**Get proposed schema changes as a patch.**

```{r}
patch <- schema_patch(run$conformance, NULL, run$cells, run$schema)
patch$enum_additions
```

A value that appears many times probably needs adding to the schema. A value
that appears once is probably a typo. The patch only proposes adding the
values that appear many times.

## Requirements

- R >= 4.0
- [ecoextract](https://github.com/n8layman/ecoextract) output, or any record
  table plus the `schema.json` it was extracted against
- An API key for the AI reviewer: copy `.env.example` to `.env`. Without one,
  the plain comparisons still run, and cells they can't settle are counted as
  differences until the AI reviewer reads them.
